screens.title: News Feed — Fanout Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Delivering posts from creators to followers is the core challenge of a news feed. In this lesson we examine three practical fanout strategies — push, pull, and hybrid — and learn how they trade latency for storage and computation. You will see why push-on-write gives instant reads but multiplies writes, why pull-on-read avoids write amplification at the cost of slower reads, and how hybrid systems balance both approaches by treating high-follower and low-follower authors differently. We will also unpack the role of message queues and background workers that make fanout safe and resilient, and review the common mistakes that lead to overload: ignoring backpressure, skipping caching, or using a single strategy for all users. By the end you will be able to pick a fanout approach given a user distribution, read-to-write ratio, and latency target, and you will sketch a hybrid decision rule based on follower thresholds. Consider an influencer with millions of followers versus an ordinary user with a few dozen followers — the right strategy differs, and that is precisely what we will explore.

screens.title: Push-based Fanout (Fanout-on-Write)
screens.narratorSegment: Push-based fanout writes a new post into each follower’s personalized inbox at the moment the post is created. The essential claim is simple: precompute the user's feed once and read it instantly later. Concretely, when an author publishes, the Post Service stores the post and emits an event. A fanout worker consumes that event, fetches the author's follower list, and writes a denormalized copy into every follower's feed table. This yields very low read latency because reads are simple lookups. A concrete example: if an influencer with 100,000 followers posts, each follower’s inbox receives a copy so that later reads are O(1). The main trade-off is write amplification: a single logical post becomes many physical writes. A common misconception is to assume push always reduces cost — it reduces read time but increases storage and write throughput. Mitigations include asynchronous queues, sharded worker pools, and special-casing extremely large follower lists with alternative strategies. Key takeaway: push favors user experience at read time but shifts cost to write-time processing and storage. Ask yourself: which side of the read/write cost curve is my application on?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Push-based Fanout
Core Concept
Push-based Fanout
Precompute follower inboxes when a post is created.
How it works
  • Post Service stores post and publishes an event.
  • Fanout worker reads event and fetches follower list.
  • Worker writes the post into each follower's inbox (denormalized).
Concrete example
An author with 100,000 followers causes 100,000 writes to user_feed storage when publishing once; later reads are direct lookups.
Key Takeaway

Push trades write cost for read speed. Prepare for write throughput, storage, and backpressure handling.

Common mistakes
  • Not using queues or rate-limited workers; fanout can overwhelm the DB.
  • Trying to push for every user uniformly regardless of follower count.
  • Omitting monitoring for backpressure and retry failures.
Pro tip
Use asynchronous queues and shard work by follower ranges. Consider special handling for extremely large accounts.
Reflection
If your users read much more than they write, push improves perceived performance despite extra writes. Is that true for your product?

screens.title: Push Fanout — Worker Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A robust push implementation follows a predictable pipeline: post, publish event, queue, fanout worker, follower lookup, and denormalized writes. Start with the Post Service: validate and store the post, then publish a NewPostEvent to a message queue. The queue decouples writers from fanout consumers and smooths spikes. Fanout workers subscribe to the queue and perform follower lookups from the Follower Service. For each follower the worker writes a compact feed entry to a user_feed store. Use batching and sharding: group writes by target partition and apply parallel workers per shard. Handle failures with idempotent writes, per-message retries, and dead-letter queues for persistent errors. A concrete scenario: thousands of posts per second require multiple queue partitions and worker groups; each worker processes a follower range and writes batched inserts to the feed store. A common misconception is that worker scale-out alone solves overload; without batching, rate limiting, and backpressure signals, you will exhaust storage IOPS. The takeaway is to treat fanout as a streaming job with careful operational controls: batching, retries, sharding, and metrics. Push Fanout — Worker Workflow means use queues, batches, sharding, and idempotent workers to make push fanout reliable and scalable.. In practical terms, step-by-step fanout pipeline from post to inboxes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Fanout Worker Pipeline
A reliable push flow uses queues and resilient worker logic.
1. Post Service
Validate and store post; emit NewPostEvent to queue.
2. Message Queue
Partition events to enable parallel consumers and smoothing spikes.
3. Fanout Workers
Consume events, fetch followers, batch writes to feed storage.
Operational controls
  • Batch writes and group by storage shard to reduce IOPS.
  • Use idempotent writes and sign events for safe retries.
  • Monitor queue length and backpressure; use rate limits and circuit breakers.
Concrete scenario
If 5,000 posts arrive per second, partition the queue, run shard-specific workers, and write in batches to avoid saturating the feed DB.

screens.narratorSegment: Reading the pseudocode helps make operational choices explicit. A fanout worker consumes a NewPostEvent, retrieves follower IDs, groups them into batches by storage shard, and performs idempotent inserts into each follower's feed. Important implementation details include batching for throughput, marking entries with the original post id to avoid duplicates, and using last-applied markers or unique constraints to make retries safe. A concrete example walkthrough: receive event with post_id and author_id, fetch 10,000 followers, break them into batches of 500, and write to five shards in parallel. Common misconceptions include treating the pseudocode as a single-threaded loop — a production worker parallelizes batches and responds to backpressure from the storage layer. Also, do not store large post blobs in each inbox; keep compact references and read full content from the Posts store when needed. The takeaway: pseudocode clarifies the right knobs to tune—batch size, parallelism, idempotency, and error handling—so your push system remains reliable under spikes. Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Push — Pseudocode
Fanout Worker — Pseudocode
A clear, readable structure with batching and idempotency.
# pseudocode (conceptual)
def handle_event(event):
  post_id = event['post_id']
  author_id = event['author_id']
  followers = get_followers(author_id)  # may be paginated

  for batch in chunk(followers, size=500):
    grouped = group_by_shard(batch)
    parallel_write(grouped, post_id)

  # Ensure writes are idempotent using unique keys or last-applied markers
Key implementation notes
  • Use compact feed entries with post_id and timestamp, not full body.
  • Batch and parallelize writes to match storage partitions.
  • Make writes idempotent for safe retries; use a dead-letter queue for failures.
Misconception
Horizontal scaling without batching often hits IOPS limits. Batching reduces per-write overhead dramatically.
Takeaway
Design worker logic as a streaming, partitioned job with clear retry and batching policies.

screens.title: Pull-based Fanout (Fanout-on-Read)
screens.narratorSegment: Pull-based fanout assembles a user's feed at read time by querying the authors they follow and merging recent posts. The claim here is that writes remain simple — each post is written once to the main Posts store — and reads do the work of aggregation. A concrete example: a user follows 200 accounts; when they request their feed, the Feed Service fetches recent posts for each followee, merges and sorts them by timestamp, and returns the top N. This model avoids write amplification because one post produces a single physical write. However, it can incur high read latency and read amplification when a user follows thousands of accounts. Caching is the critical mitigation: aggressively cache aggregated results or each author's recent posts, and refresh caches based on write patterns. A common misconception is that pull is always cheaper — it is cheaper for writes but can cost a lot in C P U and latency for heavy readers. The takeaway: pull is a good fit when writes dominate or follower graphs are shallow, but it requires careful caching to be viable at scale.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Pull-based Fanout
Core Concept
Pull-based Fanout
Aggregate posts from followees at request time.
How it works
  • Post Service stores post once in Posts DB.
  • On a feed request, fetch followee list, query recent posts per followee, merge and sort.
  • Return top N posts to the user.
Concrete example
A user follows 200 people. The feed service fetches recent posts for each followee, merges them, and returns the newest 20 items.
Performance concerns
  • High read latency for users who follow many accounts.
  • Read amplification: many small queries to the Posts store per feed request.
  • Caching is essential: cache per-author recent posts or cached aggregated feeds.
Takeaway
Pull avoids write amplification but requires cache strategy to keep reads fast for heavy-follow users.

screens.title: Pull Fanout — Feed Retrieval Steps
screens.narratorSegment: A pull feed retrieval is a short pipeline but can expand into many queries. First, when a user requests their feed, the Feed Service queries the Follower Service to obtain the list of authors this user follows. Second, for each followee the service fetches recent posts from the Posts DB or a per-author cache. Third, it merges and sorts all candidate posts by timestamp and applies ranking or filtering, then returns the top N to the client. Critical caching points include per-author recent-post caches and a short-lived aggregated cache for frequently requested feeds. A concrete example: a user follows 5,000 authors; without caching the Feed Service might issue thousands of queries, leading to high latency. A common mistake is to cache only individual posts rather than aggregated results; while per-author caches help, aggregated caches reduce merge cost significantly for heavy readers. The takeaway: design both per-author and aggregated caches with appropriate TTLs and invalidation strategies to make pull feasible under load. Feed Retrieval Steps
Where to cache and when to fetch from primary stores.
1. Get followee list
Query Follower Service; consider caching follower sets for active users.
2. Fetch recent posts
Use per-author caches or Posts DB reads; batch and parallelize fetches.
3. Merge, sort, return
Aggregate posts, sort by timestamp or rank, apply deduplication, and return the top N.
Caching strategy
Cache per-author recent posts and maintain short-lived aggregated caches for active feeds to avoid repeated merges.
Common mistake
Failing to cache aggregated results forces the Feed Service to re-run expensive merges for every request.

screens.narratorSegment: A pull-model pseudocode clarifies where caching reduces work. The feed function first retrieves the followee list and then attempts to load an aggregated cache entry. If the aggregated cache is missing, it loads recent posts for each followee, merges, sorts, and populates the aggregated cache for a short TTL. Example flow: attempt aggregated cache for user U; miss; load cached recent posts for each followee where available; for any cache miss fetch from Posts DB; merge, sort, and return top N while priming caches. Misconceptions include assuming per-author caches alone are sufficient; they reduce some work but still require merging. Real systems also lazily refresh aggregated caches when writers post or when cache TTL expires. The takeaway: the pull code makes explicit caching decision points—cache hits short-circuit expensive merges, and cache priming reduces latency for heavy readers. Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Pull — Pseudocode
Pull Model — Pseudocode
Explicit cache checks reduce merge costs.
# pseudocode (conceptual)
def get_feed(user_id, limit=20):
  followees = get_followees(user_id)

  # Try aggregated cache first
  cached = get_aggregated_cache(user_id)
  if cached:
    return cached[:limit]

  # Otherwise fetch per-author recent posts (prefer cache)
  candidates = []
  for a in followees:
    recent = get_author_cache(a) or get_posts_by_user(a, count=limit)
    candidates.extend(recent)

  candidates.sort(key=lambda p: p['timestamp'], reverse=True)
  result = candidates[:limit]
  set_aggregated_cache(user_id, result, ttl=30)
  return result
Where caching helps
  • Aggregated feed cache for active users.
  • Per-author recent posts cache to avoid DB calls.
  • Short TTLs and opportunistic refresh on writes.
Misconception
Relying only on per-author caches still forces costly merges for many followees. Aggregated cache wins when a feed is requested frequently.

screens.title: Write vs Read Amplification
screens.narratorSegment: Write amplification and read amplification are two complementary costs when designing feeds. Write amplification occurs when a single logical write is expanded into many physical writes, typical of push systems. Read amplification happens when a single feed request triggers many database reads, typical of naive pull designs. To reason about them, estimate the follower distribution and read-to-write ratio. For example, if an author has 1M followers, a single post creates one million writes; that is heavy write amplification. Conversely, if a user follows 10,000 accounts and requests a feed frequently, each request can trigger many reads, causing high read amplification. Mitigations differ by model: for push, use batching, background workers, and special-case extremely large accounts; for pull, use per-author and aggregated caching, batched fetches, and pagination to limit immediate work. Write vs Read Amplification
Compare costs and mitigations for both amplification types.
Write Amplification (Push)
  • One post becomes N writes to follower inboxes.
  • Mitigate with batching, sharding, and queue-based workers.
  • Special-case extremely large follower counts.
Read Amplification (Pull)
  • A single feed request triggers many reads across authors.
  • Mitigate with per-author and aggregated caches, batching, and TTL tuning.
  • Use pagination and early stopping to reduce work for top N results.
Operational note

screens.title: Hybrid Fanout — Decision Flow
screens.narratorSegment: A hybrid fanout applies push for high-impact authors and pull for low-impact ones, balancing write and read costs. The architecture requires a decision point in the Fanout Service: when consuming a NewPostEvent, check the author's follower count. If it exceeds a configured threshold, the worker performs push fanout to the followers’ inboxes; otherwise, the system relies on pull and may warm a per-author cache. When a user requests their feed, the Feed Service reads the precomputed inbox entries (those pushed) and also pulls recent posts from followees designated as pull-only, then merges and de-duplicates the combined list. Implementation details include choosing the threshold (for example, 10,000 followers), ensuring merging handles duplicates and ordering, and applying caching to pulled subsets. A common misconception is that hybrid removes complexity; it actually increases it because you must maintain two code paths and merging logic. The practical payoff is a large reduction in total writes while keeping low read latency for followers of hot authors. The final design decision comes from measuring follower skew and user latency targets. In practical terms, combine push and pull using follower thresholds and mixed feeds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Message Queues & Background Workers
screens.narratorSegment: Message queues and background workers are the glue that make fanout safe and non-blocking. The Post Service should publish NewPostEvents to a durable queue so writers return quickly while work is processed asynchronously. Consumers read events and execute fanout logic. Important patterns include partitioning queues so consumers can scale horizontally, using idempotent processing to tolerate retries, and employing dead-letter queues for events that repeatedly fail. Backpressure handling is crucial: when the downstream feed store is saturated, the queue will grow; workers should expose metrics and autoscale, and the system should consider throttling producers or falling back to a pull approach for some events. A concrete example: when queues exceed thresholds, mark very large authors for delayed fanout or temporarily move them to pull-path to avoid meltdown. Common mistakes include ignoring consumer lag, not setting appropriate TTLs on queue messages, or failing to design idempotent consumers. The takeaway: design the queue-and-worker subsystem as a resilient streaming pipeline with observability and fallback strategies. Message Queues and Background Workers
Patterns for durability, scaling, and failure handling.
Durability & partitioning
Use durable queues, partition topics so consumers can process subsets in parallel, and maintain consumer offsets.
Idempotency & retries
Design worker writes to be safe to retry. Use unique keys or last-applied markers and dead-letter queues for persistent failures.
Backpressure & fallbacks
Monitor queue lag and write latency. If overloaded, throttle producers, scale consumers, or temporarily route to pull path for some authors.

Set alerts on queue length and consumer lag. Automate scaling and define a safe fallback when thresholds are breached.

screens.title: Design a Hybrid Fanout Logic Flow
screens.narratorSegment: This activity asks you to design the high-level logic for a hybrid fanout system with a push threshold of 10,000 followers. For the Post Service, the steps are straightforward: accept and validate the post, store it in the Posts store, and publish a NewPostEvent containing post_id and author_id to a durable queue. For the Fanout Service, the worker consumes the event, queries the follower count for the author, and branches: if follower_count is greater than 10,000, perform push fanout by fetching follower IDs and writing entries into their inboxes using batched, idempotent writes; if follower_count is less or equal, skip mass writes and let followers see the post via pull logic. Optionally warm a per-author cache for recent posts to speed reads. Important operational considerations include partitioning the queue, batching follower writes, handling retries idempotently, and monitoring queue lag to trigger fallbacks. One misconception to avoid is assuming a fixed threshold is always right; thresholds must be revisited with real metrics. The core insight is that this hybrid rule reduces total writes while preserving low-latency delivery for the most-followed authors.

fullNarratorScript:
Delivering posts from creators to followers is the core challenge of a news feed. In this lesson we examine three practical fanout strategies — push, pull, and hybrid — and learn how they trade latency for storage and computation. You will see why push-on-write gives instant reads but multiplies writes, why pull-on-read avoids write amplification at the cost of slower reads, and how hybrid systems balance both approaches by treating high-follower and low-follower authors differently. We will also unpack the role of message queues and background workers that make fanout safe and resilient, and review the common mistakes that lead to overload: ignoring backpressure, skipping caching, or using a single strategy for all users. By the end you will be able to pick a fanout approach given a user distribution, read-to-write ratio, and latency target, and you will sketch a hybrid decision rule based on follower thresholds. Consider an influencer with millions of followers versus an ordinary user with a few dozen followers — the right strategy differs, and that is precisely what we will explore.

In these objectives you will build practical judgment about fanout trade-offs and the system components involved. First, you will learn to name and differentiate push, pull, and hybrid fanout strategies, and explain when each reduces latency or cost. Second, you will analyze trade-offs: understand write amplification, read amplification, and where complexity grows. Third, you will practice deciding a strategy based on workload: given follower distributions and read-to-write ratios, you’ll select push, pull, or hybrid approaches. Fourth, you will implement and reason about message queues and background workers to perform safe fanout without overwhelming storage or losing events. Each skill matters because real-world feeds combine different user patterns; knowing which strategy to apply prevents outages and keeps latency predictable. As you work through examples, consider a celebrity post versus a casual user's post and the impact on writes, reads, and storage. These objectives set the stage for designing a hybrid rule and implementing resilient fanout services.

These objectives frame practical exercises and verification steps you will use. You will practice diagnosing a workload: measure follower distributions and the read-to-write ratio, then predict whether push or pull is more cost-effective. You will also design a hybrid rule and explain its correctness: set a follower threshold, describe merging logic, and identify caching points. Next, you will outline reliable fanout flows using message queues and background workers, and specify retry and backpressure strategies. Finally, you will defend your choice with a short trade-off summary: what you gained in read latency and what you paid in storage or complexity. Doing these activities trains the judgment you need in interviews: selecting an approach is rarely binary; it’s about making clear trade-offs and engineering mitigations. Expect to produce small diagrams, a pseudocode sketch, and a one-paragraph rationale for your chosen threshold.

Push-based fanout writes a new post into each follower’s personalized inbox at the moment the post is created. The essential claim is simple: precompute the user's feed once and read it instantly later. Concretely, when an author publishes, the Post Service stores the post and emits an event. A fanout worker consumes that event, fetches the author's follower list, and writes a denormalized copy into every follower's feed table. This yields very low read latency because reads are simple lookups. A concrete example: if an influencer with 100,000 followers posts, each follower’s inbox receives a copy so that later reads are O(1). The main trade-off is write amplification: a single logical post becomes many physical writes. A common misconception is to assume push always reduces cost — it reduces read time but increases storage and write throughput. Mitigations include asynchronous queues, sharded worker pools, and special-casing extremely large follower lists with alternative strategies. Key takeaway: push favors user experience at read time but shifts cost to write-time processing and storage. Ask yourself: which side of the read/write cost curve is my application on?

A robust push implementation follows a predictable pipeline: post, publish event, queue, fanout worker, follower lookup, and denormalized writes. Start with the Post Service: validate and store the post, then publish a NewPostEvent to a message queue. The queue decouples writers from fanout consumers and smooths spikes. Fanout workers subscribe to the queue and perform follower lookups from the Follower Service. For each follower the worker writes a compact feed entry to a user_feed store. Use batching and sharding: group writes by target partition and apply parallel workers per shard. Handle failures with idempotent writes, per-message retries, and dead-letter queues for persistent errors. A concrete scenario: thousands of posts per second require multiple queue partitions and worker groups; each worker processes a follower range and writes batched inserts to the feed store. A common misconception is that worker scale-out alone solves overload; without batching, rate limiting, and backpressure signals, you will exhaust storage IOPS. The takeaway is to treat fanout as a streaming job with careful operational controls: batching, retries, sharding, and metrics. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A concrete example walkthrough: receive event with post_id and author_id, fetch 10,000 followers, break them into batches of 500, and write to five shards in parallel. Common misconceptions include treating the pseudocode as a single-threaded loop — a production worker parallelizes batches and responds to backpressure from the storage layer. Pull-based fanout assembles a user's feed at read time by querying the authors they follow and merging recent posts. The claim here is that writes remain simple — each post is written once to the main Posts store — and reads do the work of aggregation. A concrete example: a user follows 200 accounts; when they request their feed, the Feed Service fetches recent posts for each followee, merges and sorts them by timestamp, and returns the top N. This model avoids write amplification because one post produces a single physical write. However, it can incur high read latency and read amplification when a user follows thousands of accounts. Caching is the critical mitigation: aggressively cache aggregated results or each author's recent posts, and refresh caches based on write patterns. A common misconception is that pull is always cheaper — it is cheaper for writes but can cost a lot in C P U and latency for heavy readers. The takeaway: pull is a good fit when writes dominate or follower graphs are shallow, but it requires careful caching to be viable at scale.

A pull feed retrieval is a short pipeline but can expand into many queries. First, when a user requests their feed, the Feed Service queries the Follower Service to obtain the list of authors this user follows. Second, for each followee the service fetches recent posts from the Posts DB or a per-author cache. Third, it merges and sorts all candidate posts by timestamp and applies ranking or filtering, then returns the top N to the client. Critical caching points include per-author recent-post caches and a short-lived aggregated cache for frequently requested feeds. A concrete example: a user follows 5,000 authors; without caching the Feed Service might issue thousands of queries, leading to high latency. A common mistake is to cache only individual posts rather than aggregated results; while per-author caches help, aggregated caches reduce merge cost significantly for heavy readers. The takeaway: design both per-author and aggregated caches with appropriate TTLs and invalidation strategies to make pull feasible under load. This activity asks you to design the high-level logic for a hybrid fanout system with a push threshold of 10,000 followers. For the Post Service, the steps are straightforward: accept and validate the post, store it in the Posts store, and publish a NewPostEvent containing post_id and author_id to a durable queue. For the Fanout Service, the worker consumes the event, queries the follower count for the author, and branches: if follower_count is greater than 10,000, perform push fanout by fetching follower IDs and writing entries into their inboxes using batched, idempotent writes; if follower_count is less or equal, skip mass writes and let followers see the post via pull logic. Here are the three essential ideas to hold onto. First, fanout determines where work happens: push moves work to write time for fast reads, while pull moves work to read time to save writes. Second, amplification is the lens for cost: write amplification multiplies storage and IOPS during push, read amplification multiplies query work during pull; measure follower skew and request patterns to quantify these costs. Third, hybrid is pragmatic: apply push to hot authors and pull to cold ones, but accept the added complexity of merging and de-duplication. For operational systems, queues, batching, idempotent workers, and caching are the practical levers that make these strategies safe and performant.
